extracted.intended_audience: statesmen, founders of states, students and readers of political philosophy
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and evaluative principles about the causes of corruption and the means of preservation for different forms of government (monarchies, tyrannies, oligarchies, democracies). Targeted at those who would found, correct, or govern a state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between a kingdom (king) and a tyranny (tyrant)
rubrics_metrics.description: A kingdom is bestowed according to worth — virtue, family, beneficent actions, or power — and the king's end is the protection and honour of his people; a tyrant is chosen from the meaner populace, is an enemy to the better sort, and his sole object is pleasure and wealth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicators: appointment origins (virtue, descent, benefaction vs demagogue/populace support), aims (honour/guardian vs pleasure/wealth), and guards (king's guards are citizens; tyrant's are foreigners). Examples: Codrus, Cyrus as founders; many tyrants originated as demagogues (e.g., Pisistratus, Cypselus).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tyranny as the fusion of democracy's and oligarchy's worst traits
rubrics_metrics.description: A tyranny partakes of the worst of both democracy and oligarchy, retaining corruptions and defects of both forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From oligarchy it takes a pursuit of gain (to buy guards, luxuries) and distrust of the people (depriving them of arms); from democracy it takes enmity toward the nobles and destructive persecution or banishment of eminent citizens. This hybridity helps explain its particular vulnerabilities and behaviors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causes of conspiracies against monarchs and tyrants
rubrics_metrics.description: Principal causes that induce conspiracies: injurious contempt, deprivation of private fortunes, fear of punishment, hatred, anger, and contempt arising from improper conduct or insults.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contempt (being despised or held in low esteem) is singled out as especially powerful; personal insults (sexual affronts, scourging, public humiliation) and fear of punishment provoke plots. Examples: Harmodius and Aristogiton against Pisistratus's family; Pausanias against Philip; conspiracies by generals who despise effemacy or weakness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hatred and contempt as chief motives for overthrow
rubrics_metrics.description: Hatred is often inseparable from tyrants and is powerful; contempt frequently leads to destruction—those who despise a ruler are more ready to conspire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish anger (accompanied by grief and less rational) from hatred (more persistent). Many historical overthrows trace back to contempt or hatred caused by insults, disgrace, or violations of honour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stability through moderation of royal power
rubrics_metrics.description: The stability of a kingdom depends on keeping the king's power within moderate bounds; the less extensive his power, the longer the government will continue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reducing despotism and preserving a degree of equality lessens envy and conspiracy. Example: The Molossi and Lacedaemonians (division of power, ephori instituted by Theopompus) — diminishing absolute power makes the kingdom more durable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preservation of tyranny by impoverishing and isolating the populace
rubrics_metrics.description: A durable tyranny is maintained by keeping citizens poor, preventing mutual confidence, and denying them the means to form a guard or conspiracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical measures: forbid public meals/clubs/education/learned meetings; force strangers to live by the gate; employ spies/listeners; multiply taxes; confiscate private property; encourage war to occupy them; use foreign guards. Examples: Pyramids and public works used to keep people poor; Dionysius' collection of private property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preservation of tyranny by appearing kingly and respectable
rubrics_metrics.description: The opposite method of preserving a tyranny is to make the government seem kingly — to secure submission (even unwilling) through apparent guardianship of the public good and maintenance of power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical measures: appear to attend to public finances and to keep public money for state exigencies, be respectable (veneration rather than fear), show religion and respect to men of merit, distribute honours personally but let subordinate officers issue censures, avoid sudden concentration of large power in an ardent individual, and gradually remove dangerous powers. Avoid hypocrisy in piety and overt insolence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid corporal punishment and public disgrace of men of honour
rubrics_metrics.description: Never exercise corporal punishment over those with a delicate sense of honour; if punishment is necessary, it should be like a father's correction, not contemptuous; restore honour by bestowing greater honours when possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Men of honour are easily moved by disgrace; physical humiliation provokes deep resentment and conspiracy. Prefer non-contemptuous correction and recompense with honour to pacify offended elites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding the appearance of indulgence and vice
rubrics_metrics.description: A ruler should not appear given to sensual pleasures, drunkenness, or sluggardliness; such appearances invite contempt and plots.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if indulging in pleasures privately, appear moderate or abstinent in public. The drunkard and sluggard are more exposed to contempt than the sober and industrious ruler.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of spies and suppression of mutual confidence
rubrics_metrics.description: To prevent conspiracies, tyrants should make people strangers to each other, encourage mutual accusation, and employ spies and listeners to detect seditious talk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific practices: send out eavesdroppers (potagogides), encourage neighbours and servants to inform, and publicly place strangers near gates for surveillance. The effect is to stifle free speech and mutual plotting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manipulate social relations to prevent unity among the capable
rubrics_metrics.description: Tyrants should oppose or suppress men of merit, prevent citizens from trusting one another, and prefer foreigners/corrupt dependents to local notable citizens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep worthy men from gaining confidence or collective strength (deny honours, exclude from intimacy), prefer strangers at court and in guard duties, encourage flatterers and wretches who will not challenge the tyrant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three primary objectives of tyrannical policy
rubrics_metrics.description: The three aims tyrants pursue: (1) make citizens poor and abject, (2) prevent mutual confidence among them, (3) deprive them of the means (power) to act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All tyrannical measures (taxation, suppression of associations, use of spies, removal of property) tend toward accomplishing one of these three ends; these are diagnostic criteria for whether policy is tyrannical and effective in preserving tyranny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer delegation and prudent succession management in tyrannies
rubrics_metrics.description: Some tyrannies are preserved by delegating power from one to another and by managing succession prudently (avoid leaving hoarded wealth that tempts regents), so as to reduce incentives for regents to innovate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appear to collect taxes for the public and keep accounts; take suspected regents with you when leaving; avoid leaving large hoards that create incentives for successors to change regime; leave resources in a way that secures the continuing subservience of regents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not make one person or many persons too great in monarchy
rubrics_metrics.description: A common protection of monarchies is not to make one person too great (or too many great persons who will support each other), since they will be able to support each other in revolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If it is necessary to entrust large powers, avoid choosing ardent-spirited men; remove dangerous powers gradually rather than abruptly; fragment authority to prevent concentrated opposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attach both rich and poor by equal protection and ally with most powerful party
rubrics_metrics.description: A ruler should ensure that both rich and poor find equal protection, and attach to himself the party which is the most powerful so he need not disarm citizens or make slaves free.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balancing protections prevents one class from dominating the other and reduces the likelihood of conspiracy; securing the support of the most powerful faction provides material means to deter revolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation and legal obedience prolong oligarchic/tyrannical rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Oligarchies and tyrannies last longer when rulers use power with moderation and are obedient to laws or customary practices that make their rule appear legitimate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Orthagoras and Cypselus families maintained rule by moderation and popular measures (e.g., governing without guards). Popular measures and apparent legality reduce contempt and conspiracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democracy's foundation: liberty as governing and being governed alternately
rubrics_metrics.description: The foundation of a democratic state is liberty; one principal part of this liberty is that citizens govern and are governed in turn — equality in democracy is measured by numbers, not by worth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Norms: supreme power vested in the people at large; majority decisions final; the poor (as the greater number) rightly claim greater power. Another articulated democratic right is 'to live as one likes.' This defines the democratic ideal but also points to potential excesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democratic equality criterion: numerical equality over merit
rubrics_metrics.description: In democratic justice equality is measured by numbers rather than worth; entitlement and political power derive from numerical majority rather than superior merit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: offices and honors are distributed according to rotation and numerical equality, not exclusive rights of the virtuous or wealthy. This is a defining evaluative standard for democratic constitutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different species of democracies depend on population makeup and attached practices
rubrics_metrics.description: There are many species of democracy because populations differ (husbandmen, mechanics, hired servants) and because various practices (what attends the democracy) are joined to the state, which changes its character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Founders or correctors of states should examine particulars: the social composition and the set of institutions linked to the democratic form (deliberative assemblies, magistracy election, judicial arrangements) to determine which democratic model fits a particular city.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixed constitutions arise from mismatched departmental organization
rubrics_metrics.description: Combinations of governmental parts (deliberative, electoral, judicial) regulated in manners corresponding to different forms (oligarchy, aristocracy, democracy) produce mixed governments that alter the character of the state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate each department separately: e.g., if the deliberative department is oligarchic while election of magistrates is aristocratic, the resulting polity will be a hybrid; understanding these mixes is essential when diagnosing or designing constitutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causes of regime change: internal assumptions of power and external pressures
rubrics_metrics.description: Regimes are overthrown either internally when those in power assume greater authority than the law allows or when powerful neighbors or opposing principles desire to subvert the state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Internal causes: sedition by those in power, efforts to become tyrannical (assumption of unauthorized powers), insolence of hereditary rulers. External causes: neighbor-states with opposed principles (e.g., democracies opposing tyrannies) or opportunistic foreign intervention.
